findings.headline: SEND specialist education placement provision costing £36.130m for 696 children, with external specialist placement funding overspending by £2.669m
findings.detail: The council maintained 696 children in specialist education placements costing £36.130m at the end of March 2026. External SEND specialist placements overspent by £2.669m due to increased demand for pupils with complex needs where mainstream schools cannot meet their needs. Special school top-up funding also overspent by £1.785m to meet increasing severity of need.
findings.matters: The scale and growth of specialist SEND provision costs are material to overall council finances; lenders and peer finance officers need to understand demand trajectory and how costs are funded
findings.figures: £36.130m for 696 children; £2.669m external specialist placement overspend; £1.785m special school top-up overspend
findings.quote: At the end of March 2026 there were 696 children in specialist education placements costing £36.130m. External SEND specialist placements have overspent by £2.669m due to an increase in demand for those pupils with complex needs, where mainstream schools cannot meet need.

findings.headline: EHC plan funding overspent by £10.709m (25.9% of budget), with Lincolnshire's rate 15 per cent above national and 30 per cent above regional average
findings.detail: Top-up and targeted funding for children with Education and Health Care plans overspent by £10.709m (25.9% of budget). Lincolnshire's EHC plan rate of 6.1% of the school population significantly exceeds both national average (15% higher) and regional average (30% higher). The EHC plan growth rate increased 10% from the prior year.
findings.matters: This reveals structural SEND identification and funding patterns significantly above peer councils, signalling systemic challenges in mainstream inclusion that peers should assess
findings.figures: £10.709m overspend (25.9% of budget); 6.1% EHC plan rate; 15% above national, 30% above regional average; 10% growth from prior year
findings.quote: Lincolnshire's EHC plan rate was 6.1% of the school population in 2025 which was 15% higher than national and 30% higher than the regional average. The EHC plan growth rate increased by 10% from the prior year adding further pressure to the system.

findings.headline: Council budgeted for £18.492m planned overspend on High Needs block in 2025/26
findings.detail: The council set its High Needs budget with a built-in planned overspend of £18.492m in 2025/26. Beyond this, the paper details an additional £11.567m in overspend driven by demand-led services: EHC plan funding (£10.709m), external specialist placements (£2.669m), and special school top-up funding (£1.785m), partly offset by underspends in alternative provision (£3.596m).
findings.matters: A budgeted structural overspend signals funding inadequacy in High Needs provision; finance directors and lenders need to understand how such overspends are funded and whether they are sustainable
findings.figures: £18.492m planned overspend; £30.059m total High Needs overspend; £11.567m additional overspend beyond planned
findings.quote: Even allowing for the careful management of the DSG, a focus on early intervention and transformation, and a strong financial position compared to many LAs, the Council set a budget based on a planned overspend on its High Needs block funding allocation of £18.492m in 2025/26.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Mainstream Schools Funding Consultation 2027-28
findings.headline: Affordability gap from lagged government funding requires continued sector-wide downward AWPU adjustment for 2027/28, following -0.612% reduction in 2026/27
findings.detail: An affordability gap arises because government allocates funding based on lagged pupil data: 2026/27 funding uses October 2024 census figures while councils must fund schools using the current year census (October 2025). Lincolnshire has experienced significant growth in Free School Meals and FSM Ever 6 entitlements from pandemic effects and cost-of-living pressures. In 2026/27, the council made a -0.612% downward adjustment to Age Weighted Pupil Unit (AWPU) values across the sector to address the gap. The council proposes to continue this approach for 2027/28, with 84% of responding schools supporting the sector-wide solution.
findings.matters: This represents a structural mismatch between government funding methodology and actual pupil demand that will require ongoing annual mitigation, revealing where the council's budget pressures originate and how schools funding sustainability depends on recurring sector-wide adjustments.
findings.figures: -0.612% AWPU adjustment in 2026/27; 84% of schools support continuing sector-wide AWPU adjustment approach for 2027/28
findings.quote: Lincolnshire has seen significant growth in both FSMs and FSMs Ever 6 over the years, firstly from the pandemic and latterly with the cost-of-living challenges, which has caused these affordability gaps.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Mainstream Schools Funding Consultation 2027-28
findings.headline: High Needs block projected overspend of £51.947m in 2026/27 with third annual proposal to transfer 0.5% of Schools block drawing only 31% school support
findings.detail: The council's latest forecast for 2026/27 shows a projected High Needs block overspend of £51.947m. The council is proposing a 0.5% transfer of Schools block funding to High Needs block for the third consecutive year to support SEND initiatives. Only 9 of 22 responding primary schools (41%) and 2 of 9 responding secondary schools (22%) support the proposal. Schools opposing the transfer cite ongoing financial pressures and concern that transferring funds would reduce mainstream schools' capacity to deliver early intervention and support for pupils' needs.
findings.matters: A finance director watching peers is interested in whether a council can build consensus on mitigation measures for structural overspends; the limited support (31% overall) signals difficulty in securing stakeholder agreement on sustainable solutions.
findings.figures: £51.947m High Needs projected overspend in 2026/27; 41% of primary schools support transfer, 22% of secondary schools support transfer; third annual proposal
findings.quote: The latest forecast for 2026/27 indicates a projected overspend of £51.947m.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Mainstream Schools Funding Consultation 2027-28
findings.headline: DSG deficit of £25.005m at March 2026 entered structural deficit for first time, with 90% DfE funding conditional on SEND Reform plan approval
findings.detail: Lincolnshire went into a structural DSG deficit for the first time during 2025/26. The council's DSG deficit at March 2026 is £25.005m. The DfE will fund 90% of the High Needs related portion of this deficit accrued up to end 2025/26 via the High Needs Sustainability Grant, conditional on approval of Lincolnshire's Local SEND Reform plan (submitted 18 June 2026). The Statutory Override supporting high needs spending ends at 2027/28; after that, government support will be managed within broader departmental spending limits and will not be unlimited.
findings.matters: A finance director or lender needs to understand the scale of the council's structural DSG deficit, the conditions attached to government support, and the council's position when that conditional support ends in 2027/28.
findings.figures: £25.005m DSG deficit at March 2026; 90% of High Needs deficit funded via High Needs Sustainability Grant; Statutory Override ends 2027/28
findings.quote: the DSG went into a structural deficit for the first time during 2025/26

findings.paper_title: De-delegations of Maintained Primary Schools Budgets
findings.headline: Maintained primary schools required to contribute greater of £10,000 or 50% of redundancy costs (capped at 3% of school budget) from 2027/28
findings.detail: Revised redundancy cost-sharing policy shifts more cost burden to schools. Schools must pay either the first £10,000 of each redundancy or 50% of total cost (whichever is greater), subject to a maximum of 3% of school budget share. This replaces the previous cost-sharing arrangement.
findings.matters: Cost-shifting of staffing restructuring from central budget to individual school budgets increases pressure on schools' financial resilience at a time of constrained resources
findings.figures: Greater of £10,000 or 50% of total redundancy cost; maximum 3% of school budget share
findings.quote: The greater of: The first £10,000 of each redundancy cost; or 50% of the total redundancy cost. This would be subject to a maximum contribution equivalent to 3.0% of the school's budget share

findings.paper_title: De-delegations of Maintained Primary Schools Budgets
findings.headline: Traveller education specialist support faces 95% growth in demand with funding held flat at £9.13 per pupil
findings.detail: The Ethnic Minority and Traveller Education Team supports schools on inclusion, access, language support, attendance and engagement. Traveller children registered as electively home educated nearly doubled in three years, but 2027/28 funding remains unchanged from 2026/27.
findings.matters: Growing pupil support needs may exceed available specialist capacity, creating sustainability pressure on central services during a period of constrained resources
findings.figures: Traveller children ECHE: 90 to 176 over three years; EMTET rate 2027/28: £9.13 per pupil (unchanged)
findings.quote: the number of Traveller children registered as electively home educated rising from 90 to 176 over the last three years

findings.paper_title: De-delegations of Maintained Primary Schools Budgets
findings.headline: School improvement and intervention support rate reduced from £24.74 to £21.50 per pupil (13% reduction) in 2027/28
findings.detail: Central Maintained Locality Lead Support and School Intervention funding is being cut. The team conducts desktop analysis three times yearly to risk-rate all maintained schools and academies, providing targeted school improvement visits and intervention according to assessed risk.
findings.matters: Reduces central support capacity for school improvement during a period when maintained schools face increased financial pressures and complexity
findings.figures: Rate 2026/27: £24.74 per pupil; Proposed Rate 2027/28: £21.50 per pupil

findings.paper_title: De-delegations of Maintained Primary Schools Budgets
findings.headline: Commitments previously funded from de-delegation reserves must now be reflected in annual budget allocations for 2027/28
findings.detail: Because the de-delegation reserve was depleted to cover the DSG deficit, the council is proposing to fund previously reserve-supported services through annual budget allocations to maintain system-wide school support services. This represents a structural shift from discretionary reserves to recurring commitments.
findings.matters: Demonstrates how DSG deficits force councils to move from discretionary reserves to recurring budget obligations, affecting medium-term financial planning
findings.figures: Various services being proposed for 2027/28 central funding from previously reserve-supported commitments
findings.quote: As a result, commitments previously supported from reserves must now be reflected within annual funding rates. The proposals set out in this report are intended to maintain key support services for maintained schools whilst ensuring funding arrangements remain sustainable.

findings.paper_title: De-delegations of Maintained Primary Schools Budgets
findings.headline: De-Delegation Reserve of £0.753m applied to Dedicated Schools Grant deficit in 2025/26 under statutory override requirement
findings.detail: The council's De-Delegation Reserve, which had been underspent and earmarked for maintained schools, was required under DSG Statutory Override rules to be applied to the overall DSG deficit at year-end 2025/26. Council officers challenged this interpretation with the DfE but were unsuccessful in their representation.
findings.matters: Shows significant education DSG deficit and statutory constraints preventing ring-fencing of reserves, relevant to all councils facing similar DSG pressures
findings.figures: £0.753m underspend applied to DSG deficit
findings.quote: Although the De-Delegation Reserve had an overall underspend of £0.753m at the end of the 2025/26 financial year, the LA has had no choice but to use this reserve to contribute to the overall DSG deficit.

findings.headline: Office for Budget Responsibility forecasting cumulative DSG deficits of up to £14 billion nationally by March 2028, placing Lincolnshire's deficit in a system-wide context of sector-wide structural imbalance
findings.detail: The paper notes that High Needs deficits are a national issue, with demand for EHCPs and specialist provision continuing to grow faster than available funding despite substantial national funding increases. Lincolnshire's structural deficit therefore reflects system-wide structural imbalances rather than local failure.
findings.matters: The scale of the national problem suggests individual council solutions will be insufficient without sector-wide reform, and the statutory override that shields the general fund expires in March 2028 at the same time system pressures peak
findings.figures: OBR forecast £14 billion cumulative deficits nationally by March 2028; statutory override extends to 31 March 2028
findings.quote: Despite substantial increases in national High Needs funding, rising demand for Education, Health and Care Plans (EHCPs), increasing complexity of need and growing reliance on specialist provision continue to drive expenditure growth at a rate that exceeds available funding.

findings.headline: Central School Services Block historic funding will be insufficient to meet PFI contract costs from 2032 onwards, creating a known structural funding gap
findings.detail: The council is currently using CSSB historic funding to offset PFI affordability commitments for special schools. CSSB historic funding reduces by 20% annually, but PFI contracts extend to August 2032. Once historic funding is exhausted, the remaining PFI costs will need to be funded from the High Needs block.
findings.matters: A known structural funding gap starting in 2032 will require either service change or reallocation from other High Needs activity, neither currently planned and both carrying delivery risk in a system already under stress
findings.figures: CSSB historic funding reduces 20% annually; PFI contracts run to August 2032; £0.753m de-delegated reserve drawn in 2025-26
findings.quote: However, as CSSB historic commitment funding reduces by 20% each year and the PFI contract remains in place until August 2032, there will be insufficient historic funding available to meet the full cost of this commitment. At that point, the remaining cost will need to be funded from the High Needs block, creating additional financial pressure on the DSG High Needs budget.

findings.headline: High Needs Sustainability Grant of £22.505m is conditional on DfE approval of the Council's Local SEND Reform Plan, representing the council's primary mechanism for managing the 2026-27 deficit
findings.detail: The grant would cover 90% of the historic High Needs deficit at 31 March 2026 but requires DfE approval of reform plans. The council acknowledges the grant provides short-term relief but does not address the structural imbalance between High Needs funding and expenditure.
findings.matters: A material funding solution covering approximately 42% of the current 2026-27 overspend is conditional on external approval and reform delivery, creating uncertainty about deficit management if approval is not granted
findings.figures: £22.505m conditional grant; represents 90% of historic High Needs deficit; approximately 42% of 2026-27 forecast overspend
findings.quote: It is anticipated that the High Needs Sustainability Grant will provide £22.505m of funding to support the High Needs deficit should the Council's Local SEND Reform Plan receive approval from the DfE.

findings.headline: 2026-27 High Needs block forecast overspend has increased from £34.5m planned to £54.071m, showing accelerating demand-driven costs
findings.detail: Despite a planned overspend being built into the budget, the latest forecast shows High Needs costs escalating faster than anticipated. Overall DSG is forecast to overspend by £53.436m. The growth is driven by rising demand for EHCPs, increasing complexity of need, and increasing reliance on specialist provision.
findings.matters: The acceleration in overspends after planned overspends were already built in suggests the council is losing control of a material cost base and costs are rising faster than forecast transformation can address
findings.figures: 2026-27 planned overspend £34.5m; forecast overspend £54.071m; overall DSG forecast overspend £53.436m
findings.quote: Whilst the 2026/27 budget was set with a planned overspend of £34.5 million, the latest forecast indicates the High Needs will overspend by £54.071 million, demonstrating the scale and pace of demand growth across the SEND system.

findings.headline: Lincolnshire entered structural DSG deficit for the first time in 2025-26, with cumulative deficit of £25.005m at 31 March 2026
findings.detail: The council had previously maintained a surplus DSG position but exhausted reserves to cover in-year overspends of £26.242m held centrally, resulting in structural deficit. The High Needs block overspend alone was £30.059m against £141m of funding.
findings.matters: Entry into structural deficit indicates a medium-term funding challenge that will need resolving before the statutory override expires in 2028
findings.figures: Cumulative DSG deficit £25.005m; High Needs block deficit £30.059m; net centrally-held overspend £26.242m
findings.quote: It has not been possible to meet the in-year overspend from the overall one-off DSG reserves, therefore the DSG went into a structural deficit for the first time during 2025/26.

findings.headline: SEND Hubs strategy intended to reduce high-cost placements, but benefits acknowledged as medium-to-long term while demand pressures accelerate
findings.detail: Better Belonging strategy includes 13 SEND Hubs now operational with 21 in development. Strong engagement with 145 applications for Enhanced Provision Grant programme. However, the paper explicitly states it is too early to evidence system-wide impact and full benefits are expected as hubs mature. Critically, it notes demand for services continues to grow, making hubs a long-term mitigation rather than an immediate cost control.
findings.matters: Major investment in local infrastructure intended to reduce expensive placements, but the council acknowledges the time lag between investment and financial benefit while the deficit mounts.
findings.figures: 13 SEND Hubs operational; 21 in development; 145 applications for Enhanced Provision Grant
findings.quote: However, as detailed earlier and throughout this report, demand for SEND services continues to grow, with increasing numbers of EHC needs assessments and EHCPs. As a result, SEND Hubs should be viewed as a key long-term mitigation within Lincolnshire's Better Belonging sufficiency strategy, with the full benefits expected to be realised as additional hubs become operational and provision matures across the county.

findings.headline: New special school banding framework implemented from Autumn 2026 to reduce exceptional funding volatility and improve long-term High Needs sustainability
findings.detail: Review of special school banding funding completed and new model due from Autumn 2026. Developed with special school leaders and finance colleagues, it aims to provide clearer alignment between need and resource, reduce reliance on exceptional funding arrangements, and support long-term financial sustainability of the High Needs Block.
findings.matters: Exceptional funding requests create financial volatility and unpredictability; a more transparent framework could improve budget certainty if it successfully reduces these ad-hoc requests.
findings.figures: Implementation Autumn 2026
findings.quote: A review of the Special School Banding funding framework has been progressed and concluded, with the revised funding model due to be implemented from the Autumn 2026 Term... A key ambition of the new model is to reduce reliance on exceptional funding arrangements by ensuring banding and funding more accurately reflect need from the outset.

findings.headline: EHCP annual review amendment rate of 83.2% is a significant outlier against national (64%) and regional (48.4%) benchmarks
findings.detail: Lincolnshire's annual review outcome shows 83.2% of reviews resulted in EHCP amendment, compared to 64% nationally and 48.4% regionally. The paper flags this as a significant outlier. In 2025, the council processed 8,223 annual reviews, of which 6,543 (approximately 80%) resulted in amendment. The paper notes this creates substantial operational demand and suggests issues with either initial assessment quality, local practice variation, or genuine changes in need.
findings.matters: Unusually high amendment rates indicate either systemic quality/practice issues or uncontrolled need escalation, both of which drive unpredictable costs and operational burden.
findings.figures: 83.2% (Lincolnshire); 64% (national); 48.4% (regional); 6,543 out of 8,223 reviews amended in 2025 (approximately 80%)
findings.quote: This places Lincolnshire as a significant outlier when compared with both regional and national benchmarks. Whilst annual reviews are intended to consider progress, provision and whether plans remain appropriate, the Children and Families Act 2014 and SEND Code of Practice are clear that EHCPs should not routinely require significant amendment each year.

findings.headline: Maintained EHCPs at 9,932 and projected to exceed 14,000 by 2030, with 44% growth since 2022
findings.detail: Education, Health and Care Plans maintained by the council have grown from 6,534 in 2022 to 9,381 in January 2026, and reached 9,932 by 30 July 2026 (a 5.9% increase since January alone). Based on current trends they are projected to exceed 14,000 by 2030. This sustained growth is identified as the most significant cost driver on the High Needs Block.
findings.matters: Rapid uncontrolled growth in EHCP numbers drives direct costs and makes medium-term financial forecasting and sustainability planning extremely difficult.
findings.quote: The number of maintained EHCPs has continued to grow. SEN2 data shows an increase from 6,534 plans in 2022 to 9,381 in 2026, representing growth of 44% over the period. Growth has continued beyond the SEN2 census date. As of 30 July 2026, Lincolnshire recorded 9,932 maintained EHCPs... Based on current trends, maintained EHCPs are projected to exceed 14,000 by 2030

findings.headline: High Needs block forecasting £51.958m in-year deficit in 2026/27, dependent on unconfirmed High Needs Sustainability grant funding
findings.detail: The High Needs Block overspent by £30.059m in 2025/26 and is forecasting a material deficit of £51.958m in 2026/27. The council expects the High Needs Sustainability grant to fund 90% (£22.505m) of the 2025/26 deficit, but this grant application remains unconfirmed, creating exposure for the authority.
findings.matters: An unresolved deficit of this scale is unsustainable and will require either significant grant funding confirmation or service/expenditure adjustments, affecting the council's overall financial position.
findings.figures: £30.059m overspend 2025/26; £51.958m forecast deficit 2026/27; £22.505m (90% of 2025/26 deficit) expected from unconfirmed grant
findings.quote: The High Needs block overspent by £30.059m in 2025/26 and is forecasting a material in-year deficit of £51.958m in 2026/27. It is expected that the High Needs Sustainability grant, once confirmed, will fund 90% (so £22.505m) of the overall DSG 2025/26 deficit.

findings.paper_title: VFM risk assessment - Lincolnshire County Council
findings.headline: Government imposed two-unitary LGR against council's single-unitary preference
findings.detail: The council submitted a Local Government Reorganisation proposal in November 2025 advocating for a single unitary authority for Lincolnshire. The government decided instead to reorganise the area into two unitary authorities. This overruling of the council's preference introduces uncertainty about future governance arrangements, service delivery models and transition costs.
findings.matters: LGR is a structural change affecting finances, governance and service continuity; councils' preferences being overridden creates execution risk and potential unexpected costs during transition that a lender must account for.
findings.figures: Decision imposed rather than negotiated; no quantified impact described
findings.quote: Although the Council's proposal advocated for a single unitary authority, the Government ultimately decided that Lincolnshire would be reorganised into two unitary authorities covering the area previously administered by Lincolnshire County Council.

findings.paper_title: VFM risk assessment - Lincolnshire County Council
findings.headline: Earmarked reserves fell £8.3m short of forecast
findings.detail: Earmarked reserves dropped from £159.3m to £125.1m, representing an adverse variance of £8.3m against the forecasted balance of £133.4m. This faster-than-planned drawdown occurred alongside the DSG moving to deficit and the General Fund remaining static at £24.2m. Despite this variance, KPMG concluded the council's strong reserve balances meant no significant financial sustainability risk.
findings.matters: Reserve drawdowns faster than forecast suggest either optimistic budgeting or emerging pressures; a lender tracks whether councils are consuming buffers faster than expected, which can signal medium-term stress.
findings.figures: Earmarked reserves £125.1m actual vs £133.4m forecast; adverse variance £8.3m; General Fund £24.2m unchanged; DSG reserve negative
findings.quote: however the reported position of £125.1m represented an adverse variance of £8.3m from the forecast reserves balance of £133.4m

findings.paper_title: VFM risk assessment - Lincolnshire County Council
findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant overspent £23m, moved to negative reserve for first time
findings.detail: The DSG overspent by £23.0 million in 2025/26, driven primarily by the High Needs Block as demand for specialist educational support and services continued to rise. 2025/26 was the first year the DSG reserve moved into negative position. The council has established arrangements to review High Needs effectiveness but the deficit persists as structural demand pressure.
findings.matters: A £23m structural overspend in a ring-fenced grant that now carries an accumulated deficit indicates sustained demand pressures the council cannot control; this creates an unfunded liability that could eventually require general fund support.
findings.figures: £23.0 million DSG overspend; High Needs Block as principal driver; first year in negative DSG reserve
findings.quote: In addition, the Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) recorded an overspend of £23.0 million. This was principally attributable to the High Needs Block, reflecting a continued increase in the number of children and young people requiring specialist educational support and services.

findings.paper_title: VFM risk assessment - Lincolnshire County Council
findings.headline: CQC rated adult social care 'Requires Improvement'; identified as significant VFM weakness
findings.detail: The Care Quality Commission assessed the Council's adult social care as 'Requires Improvement' due to governance and risk management weaknesses. The CQC found that governance structures existed but were not demonstrably effective, with risk registers not consistently linked to outcomes and governance reporting failing to show how audit findings and stakeholder feedback drove service improvements. KPMG identified this as a significant risk to the Council's ability to achieve economy, efficiency and effectiveness.
findings.matters: A major service failing to demonstrate effective governance and outcomes for vulnerable residents signals management control weaknesses; a lender needs confidence that leadership can correct substantive operational failures.
findings.figures: No quantified impact; flagged as significant VFM risk requiring follow-up audit procedures
findings.quote: Due to the findings identified by the CQC regarding the Council's adult service provision we have identified a significant risk regarding the arrangements of this service.

findings.headline: Medium-term financial plan has limited headroom beyond 2026-27 and is being reviewed mid-budget cycle.
findings.detail: The MTFP approved in February set out a balanced position but noted 'limited headroom beyond 2026/27', which was contingent on successful delivery of savings and containment of cost and demand pressures. The MTFP is now under review and will continue into autumn as part of the budget-setting process, suggesting the initial assumptions are being reassessed.
findings.matters: Limited MTFP headroom combined with demonstrated inability to manage £7.4m demand-led overspends in 2025-26 signals material medium-term budget stress. The need for savings to achieve balance rather than existing headroom indicates structural budget challenges.
findings.figures: Limited headroom beyond 2026-27; £7.442m service overspends in 2025-26; General Reserve of £24.2m (2.8% of budget requirement)
findings.quote: The MTFP, approved by Full Council in February, set out a balanced position with limited headroom beyond 2026/27, which was contingent on the successful delivery of savings and the containment of cost and demand pressures within budget assumptions at that time.

findings.headline: Financial Volatility Reserve of £46.9m now explicitly earmarked for Local Government Reorganisation costs, signalling material structural uncertainty.
findings.detail: The council amended the purpose of its Financial Volatility Reserve (£46.922m balance) to explicitly include costs arising from any future Local Government Reorganisation, with drawdowns subject to Chief Finance Officer approval. This amendment was delegated to the CFO in July 2026 and is being recommended for formal approval. The council states it will account for 'the latest assessment of financial risks' when using the reserve for LGR.
findings.matters: Explicitly reserving funds for potential LGR is a forward-looking acknowledgement that reorganisation is a material possibility. This reduces the reserve available to manage other financial shocks.
findings.figures: Financial Volatility Reserve balance £46.922m; now available for LGR costs
findings.quote: Recommendation 5 therefore seeks approval to widen the purpose of the Financial Volatility Reserve to include expenditure relating to Local Government Reorganisation, with any drawdown subject to approval by the Chief Finance Officer, in consultation with the Executive Councillor for Resources, on a case-by-case basis.

findings.headline: Capital investment 20% below plan and borrowing £46.7m less than budgeted, with the council now under-borrowed against its capital financing requirement.
findings.detail: The council invested £194.764m on capital assets, £49.656m (20%) below the £244.420m planned. Planned borrowing of £57.709m was not taken; actual borrowing was £10.961m, a variance of £46.748m (81% lower than planned). The prudential indicators show the council is under-borrowed by £103.627m against the debt liability benchmark, despite total external debt of £443.463m.
findings.matters: Capital underspend combined with borrowing shortfall could indicate either strong liquidity management or inability to execute planned investment. The under-borrowed position suggests headroom exists but financing capacity is not being deployed.
findings.figures: Capital investment £194.764m vs £244.420m planned (variance -£49.656m, -20%); borrowing £10.961m vs £57.709m planned (variance -£46.748m, -81%); under-borrowed position -£103.627m
findings.quote: The Council invested £194.764m on the County's major assets, particularly on road schemes and schools. This was £50.201m less than planned.

findings.headline: Service budget overspends of £7.4m in demand-led areas, with the council writing off carry-forwards rather than expecting to resolve these pressures.
findings.detail: Service spending (excluding schools) overspent by £7.442m (1.1% of budget). Significant overspends occurred in Children's Social Care (£4.966m or 4.1%), Adult Frailty & Long Term Conditions (£4.267m or 2.5%), and Communities (£3.189m or 3.0%). Rather than carry these overspends forward to 2026-27, the council proposes to write off the £5.334m net carry-forward, stating this avoids compounding demand-led pressures already reflected in the 2026-27 financial position.
findings.matters: Structural service budget pressures indicate the council's baseline spending commitments exceed sustainable revenue. Writing off overspends rather than addressing them signals the council expects these cost pressures to persist.
findings.figures: Service overspend £7.442m (1.1%); Children's Social Care £4.966m (4.1%); Adult Frailty £4.267m (2.5%); Communities £3.189m (3.0%); proposed write-off of £5.334m
findings.quote: Total service spending, excluding schools, was overspent by £7.442m or 1.1%... It is therefore proposed that the £5.334m net carry forward is written off, so that no service over- or underspends arising from the 2025/26 outturn are added to service budgets in 2026/27.

findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant structural deficit of £25m, dependent on government funding through a SEND reform plan the council must submit.
findings.detail: The DSG overspent by £13.406m in 2025-26 driven by High Needs block pressure. Excluding school balances, this reflects a structural deficit of £25.005m carried forward. Government will support approximately 90% of deficits to 31 March 2026, but only if the council submits an approved SEND reform plan. Any residual amount not covered by government funding must be managed through future financial planning.
findings.matters: A £25m structural deficit in schools funding is a material solvency issue that cannot be managed through annual budget monitoring. Access to government funding is contingent on external approval of a reform plan over which the council has limited control.
findings.figures: £13.406m DSG overspend in 2025-26; structural deficit of £25.005m; government support for approximately 90% of deficits to 31 March 2026
findings.quote: The Dedicated Schools Grant overspent by £13.406m, driven by continued pressure within the High Needs block. Excluding school balances, this reflects a structural deficit of £25.005m carried forward.

findings.headline: Planned £36m savings forecast to deliver £35.625m with £0.375m shortfall at Q1, with risks flagged in Legal Services and Business Support
findings.detail: Revenue budget approved by Full Council included efficiency savings of £36m. Budget Summit savings target £15.1m but forecast to deliver only £14.8m (£0.3m shortfall), largely in Adult Care and Community Wellbeing where savings remain dependent on service redesign, system changes, and workforce optimisation. Other MTFP savings target £21.5m and forecast to deliver £21.4m (£0.1m shortfall) in Resources on property rationalisation. Total shortfall £0.375m. Report flags 'risks remain within Business Support and Legal Services.' Legal Services affected by continued reliance on locums, recruitment difficulties, and uncertainty over income (£0.380m pressure).
findings.matters: Savings slippage reduces usable headroom and signals assumed productivity improvements or asset sales may not land. At quarter 1, forecasted savings already 1% adrift. With 9 months to go and delivery risks flagged, larger slippage is possible. A lender needs to know whether 2027/28 budget can be balanced without relying on similar risky savings.
findings.figures: Planned savings £36m; forecast delivery £35.625m (shortfall £0.375m or 1%); Budget Summit £15.1m planned vs £14.8m forecast; MTFP savings £21.5m planned vs £21.4m forecast; Legal Services pressure £0.380m
findings.quote: At quarter one, Budget Summit savings of £14.8m are forecast against a planned £15.1m, resulting in a £0.3m shortfall... Unachieved savings are being monitored through monthly budget holder meetings, with alternative plans required where original proposals are delayed or no longer deliverable.

findings.headline: LOBO loan of £10m with BAE Systems can be called by lender on 31 December 2026; if called, council will repay
findings.detail: Long-term debt includes LOBO loan of £10m from BAE Systems at 4%, maturing 31 December 2061. First call period falls on 31 December 2026. If lender calls the option, council will reject the lender's option to extend and will repay £10m. Fixed debt maturing in 2026/27 is £6.304m. Next call period on LOBO loans will be 31 December 2031. This possibility has been factored into cash flow for the year.
findings.matters: LOBO call removes certainty about liquidity. If BAE Systems calls option and council repays £10m, it adds to cash outflow during Q4 2026/27. Given forecast need for £33.5m external borrowing if reserves drawn, £10m LOBO repayment in December 2026 would tighten year-end liquidity.
findings.figures: LOBO loan £10m at 4% with BAE Systems; call date 31 December 2026; repayment required if called; next call dates 31 December 2031 (then every 5 years); fixed debt maturing 2026/27 £6.304m
findings.quote: Debt maturing in the year is £6.304m, however there is a possibility that an existing LOBO loan of £10m from BAE Systems may be called on 31 December 2026 and if so, this will be repaid.

findings.headline: Capital borrowing requirement increased from £82.6m to £133.4m due to carry-forward from prior year; external borrowing of £33.5m may still be needed if reserves are drawn
findings.detail: Long-term borrowing requirement for 2026/27 updated for carry-forward from 2025/26, additions and rephasing, bringing new requirement to £133.4m from original £82.6m. Capital programme underspend of £56.5m forecast to reduce to £76.98m. At this level, Debt Liability Benchmark suggests no external borrowing required to maintain £50m liquidity threshold. However, if predicted reserve use materialises, council would need to borrow approximately £33.5m in 2026/27 to maintain £50m liquidity threshold. External borrowing not to be taken until March 2027.
findings.matters: Borrowing requirement has grown significantly. Contingency on whether external borrowing needed (£33.5m) depends on reserve use actually happening—which is likely given demand pressures. A lender needs to assess headline capital financing looks manageable only if reserves do not deteriorate further.
findings.figures: Capital borrowing requirement £82.6m (budget) → £133.4m (carry-forward + additions) → £76.98m (after programme underspend); conditional external borrowing £33.5m if reserves drawn; existing long-term debt £437.18m at 3.67%; total debt if £33.5m borrowed: £470.01m at 3.75%; Capital Financing Charges 3.57% of income (vs 10% voluntary limit)
findings.quote: Long-term borrowing requirement for 2026/27 has been updated for carry forward from 2025/26, additions and rephasing of the capital programme in the quarter leaving the new requirement at £133.4m, from £82.6m... However, if predicted use of reserves takes place, as outlined in Appendix C, then this would mean that around £33.5m of external borrowing would be required to maintain the £50m liquidity threshold.

findings.headline: Total reserves forecast to fall from £137.5m to £58.4m during 2026/27, with school reserves moving into deficit
findings.detail: At 31 March 2026, total reserves stood at £137.5m. During 2026/27, forecast to reduce to £58.4m. Most significant movement in School Reserves (£43m), comprising school balances and DSG Adjustment Account holding 2025/26 deficit (£25m) and forecast 2026/27 deficit (£52m), offset by anticipated High Needs Stability Grant support for 90% of 2025/26 deficit. General Fund reserves expected to hold at £48.1m. Report notes 'forecast use of reserves provides some short-term financial resilience but does not address underlying causes of cost pressures.'
findings.matters: A reserve of £58.4m on £870m budget is just 6.7%. School reserve is in deficit and statutory. General fund reserve of £48.1m includes £24.2m General Fund (2.8% of budget) and £24m Financial Volatility Reserve (2.8%). Usable reserves limited. If demand pressures worsen or other risks materialize, council has limited headroom and would need to borrow or reduce spending.
findings.figures: Total reserves £137.5m (March 2026) → £58.4m (forecast March 2027), fall of 57%; School reserves move £43m; DSG deficit grows £25m → £54.3m; General Fund reserves £24.2m; Financial Volatility Reserve £24m
findings.quote: The total reserves balance on 31 March 2026 was £137.5m. During 2026/27, this is forecast to reduce to £58.4m... the forecast use of reserves provides some short-term financial resilience but does not address the underlying causes of cost pressures from ongoing demand and inflationary increases.

findings.headline: Core contingency budget nearly exhausted: £5.348m of £6.0m committed, leaving only £0.652m buffer plus £1.5m TROs income contingency
findings.detail: Council holds £7.5m total contingency (£6.0m core plus £1.5m TROs income offset). £5.348m committed: £2.938m for high-cost secure placements, £1.128m for SEND workforce, £0.367m for IT invest-to-save, £0.315m for emPSN exit, £0.300m Tour of Britain, £0.300m Harrowby United 3G pitch. Leaves £0.652m core contingency unallocated. TROs contingency (£1.5m) is for unachieved income and expected not to be needed in 2026/27.
findings.matters: Contingency is buffer against forecast errors and unexpected events. With Q1 already showing variances and 9 months remaining, £0.652m buffer on £799.8m budget is very tight (0.08%). Council acknowledged risks in demand-led budgets and forecast volatility. Minimal headroom if assumptions deteriorate.
findings.figures: £6.0m core contingency with £5.348m committed (89% spent); £0.652m remaining; £1.5m TROs contingency; £799.8m net revenue budget
findings.quote: Of the £6.0m core contingency, commitments totalling £5.348m are forecast... The remaining £0.7m of core contingency, together with the uncommitted TRO income contingency of £1.5m, remains unallocated at quarter one.

findings.headline: Underlying demand growth exceeds funding growth; Council explicitly states pressure is recurrent, not one-off, requiring 2027/28 budget action
findings.detail: Report explicitly states £12.6m service overspends are driven by 'pressures within demand-led budgets' and notes: 'Demand for Council services, and particularly complex demand, continues to increase at a faster rate than the Council's funding can increase.' Council acknowledges Q1 forecast shows 'Quarter two monitoring will therefore focus on identifying further mitigating actions and assessing the extent to which recurring pressures will need to be addressed through the 2027/28 budget setting process.' Not treated as timing issue but as structural mismatch.
findings.matters: A lender assesses whether deficits are recurrent or one-off. This council is signalling that demand pressures are structural and will need to be absorbed through next budget cycle. This implies either further savings, tax rises, or reserve drawdown in 2027/28.
findings.figures: £12.6m service overspends vs £7.5m contingency + other budget offsets; children's placements £11.7m pressure; transport £3.7m
findings.quote: Demand for Council services, and particularly complex demand, continues to increase at a faster rate than the Council's funding can increase. This gives rise to ongoing challenges which will need to be managed and will be a key area of focus during quarter two and as part of the budget setting exercise for 2027/28.

findings.headline: Home to School Transport overspending by £3.7m and will worsen: SEND demand growth, 6.8% transport CPI inflation, and Government has not funded the shortfall
findings.detail: Place directorate forecasting £3.7m overspend on Home to School Transport. Number of children with EHCPs continuing to increase, cost increases driven by SEND-related demand (68 additional secondary placements during Q1, Day Special transport up £0.040m alone). ONS reported transport prices rose 6.8% in 12 months to May 2026, an increase of 3% from budget-setting time. Number of supplier contract uplift requests in Q1 already matches total received in whole of previous year. Government has not allocated funding through High Needs Stability Grant to support Home to School Transport costs.
findings.matters: This is an unfunded, recurring demand pressure. SEND growth is forecast and inevitable. Transport inflation is exogenous but large. The budget cannot be controlled without reducing SEND provision (which would breach statutory duties). A lender needs to understand this is a permanent structural gap.
findings.figures: £3.684m Q1 overspend on Home to School Transport; 6.8% transport CPI inflation in 12 months to May 2026; weekly cost increase from contract re-procurements £0.077m; EHCPs increasing; no Government High Needs funding allocated to transport
findings.quote: The Place Directorate is forecasting an overspend at quarter one, largely driven by Home to School Transport overspend of £3.684m, with the service continuing to face significant financial pressure, partly driven by sustained growth and demand for SEND places... It is worth noting that the Government has not allocated any funding through the High Needs Stability Grant to support Home to School Transport costs.

findings.headline: Schools DSG deficit forecast to grow from £25m to £54.3m in a single year, with Government funding for only 90% of pre-March 2026 element
findings.detail: High Needs Block forecasting £51.96m overspend at Q1, including a planned £34.5m overspend identified during budget setting. EHCPs forecast to increase from 3,785 to 4,460, adding £8.6m pressure on mainstream top-up funding. Specialist placements at 678 vs budget assumption of 600. DSG reserve deficit expected to move from £25m end-2025/26 to £54.3m end-2026/27. Government indicated it will support approximately 90% of DSG deficits incurred up to 31 March 2026 through grant funding, with proportionate approach for deficits after that date.
findings.matters: Represents a structural financial problem for the council. Even with Government support for 90% of pre-March 2026 element, the council carries a growing deficit. The reserve is ringfenced and statutory rules prevent using general fund reserves to cover it, but it signals unsustainable SEND provision costs.
findings.figures: £25m deficit March 2026 → £54.3m deficit March 2027; £51.96m High Needs Block overspend; EHCPs: 3,785 → 4,460 (add 675); Specialist placements 678 vs budget 600; 90% Government support for pre-31 March 2026 element only
findings.quote: the forecast DSG reserve position is expected to move from a £25m deficit in March 2026 to a £54.3m deficit in March 2027, reflecting the current year overspend after allowing for anticipated High Needs Stability Grant support in respect of the 2025/26 deficit.

findings.headline: Children's independent placements overspending by £11.7m, significantly exceeding budget assumptions set in February
findings.detail: Children's Social Care is forecasting a £9.4m overspend at Q1, driven by independent placements for children in care. Detailed placement analysis shows a £11.7m cost pressure, reflecting both full-year costs of current demand and continued growth in placement numbers during remainder of 2026/27. The scale and speed of growth since October 2025 significantly exceeded assumptions built into the budget. Although FOCUS Fostering Scheme and Reunification Team delivered £5.0m of placement cost reductions exceeding the £4.7m target, this is now substantially outweighed by demand growth.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether this is one-off or recurrent. Placement demand is volatile, growing faster than the service can manage, and the budget was already substantially increased in 2026/27. If £11.7m pressure recurs next year, it signals an unfundable demand trajectory.
findings.figures: £11.7m placement cost pressure vs budget; £5.0m transformation savings achieved but overwhelmed; 58.7 per 10,000 children in care (vs 67 for statistical neighbours, 70 nationally); 93 out-of-county placements July 2026 vs 68 in October 2025
findings.quote: independent placements for Children in Care. Detailed placement analysis indicates a total independent placement cost pressure of approximately £11.7m compared with the assumptions built into the 2026/27 budget.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Council Plan Performance Framework Q1
findings.headline: Younger adults requiring residential care at 16.6 per 100,000 population, significantly below target of 27.2 per 100,000, demonstrating community-based care effectiveness
findings.detail: The council's rate of younger adults (18-64) admitted to residential and nursing care is 16.6 per 100,000, well below the target of 27.2. This exceeds target performance and demonstrates the continued effectiveness of strengths-based practice and prioritisation of community-based support. Younger adults are being enabled to live independently in their own homes and communities for longer.
findings.matters: Admission rates to residential care are cost drivers; performance significantly below target demonstrates effective community-based care delivery and cost management in a major service area despite demographic pressures
findings.figures: 16.6 per 100,000 actual vs 27.2 per 100,000 target (40% better than target)
findings.quote: Performance in Quarter 1 2026/27 was 16.6 per 100,000, exceeding the target of 27.2 per 100,000. This positive performance demonstrates the ongoing effectiveness of strengths-based practice and a commitment to maximising community-based support options.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Council Plan Performance Framework Q1
findings.headline: Children in care rate at 61.3 per 10,000 population against target of 58.7 per 10,000, above target but within tolerance and better than England and regional averages
findings.detail: Lincolnshire's rate of children in care stands at 61.3 per 10,000 children, above the 58.7 target but within the agreed tolerance range. The rate has been driven partly by the National Transfer Scheme for Unaccompanied Asylum-Seeking Children. Performance remains better than England (67), East Midlands (62) and statistical neighbours (70.8) per 10,000.
findings.matters: Children in care is a major cost driver for councils; rates above target indicate demand pressures; however, performance better than peers suggests effective management relative to comparators
findings.figures: 61.3 per 10,000 actual vs 58.7 per 10,000 target; England 67; East Midlands 62; statistical neighbours 70.8
findings.quote: At 61.3 per 10,000 under-18s, Lincolnshire's rate of Children in Care (CiC) remains above the target of 58.7 per 10,000, although performance continues to be within the agreed tolerance range. Despite this, Lincolnshire's rate remains lower than the latest published averages - England (67), East Midlands (62) and statistical neighbours (70.8) per 10,000 children (as at 31 March 2025).

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Council Plan Performance Framework Q1
findings.headline: Sickness absence above target in Adult Care and Children's Services at 10.09 and 9.45 days per FTE respectively, against council target of 8.8 days
findings.detail: Overall council sickness absence at 8.3 days per FTE is below the 8.8 day target. However, Adult Care and Community Wellbeing at 10.09 days and Children's Services at 9.45 days are both above target. Both areas are identified as having higher emotional and physical demands on staff. Managers continue to monitor absence closely and support employee wellbeing.
findings.matters: Sickness absence in key high-cost service areas signals staff stress and workload pressures; Adult Care and Children's Services represent significant council expenditure; elevated absence indicates potential service delivery and cost pressures
findings.figures: Overall 8.3 days vs 8.8 target; Adult Care 10.09 days per FTE; Children's Services 9.45 days per FTE
findings.quote: A small number of service areas are currently above target, including Adult Care and Community Wellbeing, at 10.09 days per full-time equivalent, and Children's Services, at 9.45 days per full-time equivalent. These services include roles with higher emotional and/or physical demands, which can contribute to higher levels of sickness absence than in other areas of the Council.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Council Plan Performance Framework Q1
findings.headline: Council has signed contract with Exponential-e for new SD-WAN infrastructure replacing legacy systems, with savings of £3.5m over contract term
findings.detail: The council has formally signed a contract to deliver managed SD-WAN (Software-Defined Wide Area Network) across 170+ council locations. The investment will provide more resilient, secure and cloud-ready network infrastructure while delivering significant recurring financial savings. The council has committed to £3.5m savings over the contract term.
findings.matters: Material capital investment with defined recurring savings targets; demonstrates council's capital spending and financial commitment to infrastructure modernisation
findings.figures: £3.5m savings over contract term; 170+ council locations affected
findings.quote: The Council has now formally signed the contract with Exponential-e (Expo-E) to deliver a new managed SD-WAN (Software-Defined Wide Area Network) across the authority, replacing legacy infrastructure. This investment will provide a more resilient, secure and cloud-ready network for over 170 Council locations, improving performance and reliability for staff and services while supporting future digital transformation and delivering significant recurring financial savings for the Council. As well as saving over £3.5m over the contract term.

findings.headline: Core contingency reduced to £0.7m unallocated from £6m budget after quarter one allocations to specific pressures
findings.detail: The council is allocating £5.348m of its £6m core contingency in quarter one to: £2.938m for high-cost secure placements, £1.128m for SEND workforce stabilisation, £0.367m for IT invest-to-save, £0.315m for emPSN ICO wind-down, £0.300m for Tour of Britain hosting, and £0.300m for Harrowby United stadium conversion. This leaves only £0.7m of core contingency unallocated plus a £1.5m TRO income buffer. The council notes the 'remaining contingency will need to be managed carefully during the rest of the year, given the early-stage nature of the forecast and the risk that demand-led pressures may change before outturn.'
findings.matters: With only £0.7m contingency (0.08% of net budget) remaining unallocated, the council has minimal capacity to absorb unexpected pressures during the remainder of the financial year. At quarter one, when forecasting is early-stage and demand-led budgets (social care, SEND) are volatile, this represents elevated financial risk.
findings.figures: £5.348m contingency committed in Q1; £0.7m unallocated core contingency remaining; £1.5m TRO income buffer; core contingency represents less than 1% of net budget
findings.quote: The remaining £0.7m of core contingency, together with the uncommitted TRO income contingency of £1.5m, remains unallocated at quarter one... The remaining contingency will need to be managed carefully during the rest of the year.

findings.headline: Council may require £33.5m external borrowing in March 2027 to maintain minimum liquidity threshold if reserves are used as forecast
findings.detail: Current capital programme borrowing requirement is £76.977m (after accounting for capital underspend). However, if the forecast reserve drawdowns occur as predicted in Appendix C, the council will need approximately £33.555m of external borrowing in March 2027 to maintain a £50m minimum liquidity threshold under the Debt Liability Benchmark. This borrowing would be for a 4-year term on the PWLB market. The council notes the position will be monitored throughout the year as capital rephasing and reserve usage may change.
findings.matters: This represents a material refinancing event that would lock in debt service costs for multiple years. The timing at end-March (when councils compete for PWLB funding) and the conditional nature (dependent on reserve usage in an early-stage forecast) creates both execution risk and uncertainty about the cost of refinancing.
findings.figures: £33.555m potential external borrowing requirement; 4-year PWLB term; conditional on forecast reserve usage; decision point March 2027
findings.quote: if predicted use of reserves takes place, as outlined in Appendix C, then this would mean that around £33.5m of external borrowing would be required to maintain the £50m liquidity threshold set under the liquidity benchmark.

findings.headline: LOBO loan of £10m from BAE Systems will be repaid if lender exercises call option on 31 December 2026
findings.detail: The council holds a LOBO (Lender Option Borrower Option) loan of £10m from BAE Systems at a coupon of 4% with original maturity of 31 December 2061. The call date (when lender can propose rate reset) is 31 December 2026. The council has stated it will 'reject this and repay the £10m' if the lender exercises the option. At 4%, this loan is above the council's average debt cost of 3.674%. The next call date would be 31 December 2031. The council has factored this repayment possibility into its cashflow.
findings.matters: This represents an imminent refinancing decision point. The council will need to repay £10m in December 2026 and source replacement funding at whatever market rates are available, adding to the council's overall refinancing needs in this period.
findings.figures: £10m loan amount; 4% coupon; 31 December 2026 call date; current council average debt cost 3.674%
findings.quote: This debt is at 4% and matures on 31/12/2061 however, if this call is made, we will reject this and repay the £10m.

findings.headline: Total reserves forecast to decline by £79.1m (58%) from £137.5m to £58.4m, with £43m decline in school reserves from growing DSG deficit
findings.detail: The reserve drawdown comprises school reserves declining by £43m (reflecting the DSG adjustment account moving from -£25m to -£54.3m), earmarked reserves declining by £8m, and grant reserves declining by £28m. The council notes the 'forecast use of reserves provides some short-term financial resilience but does not address the underlying causes of cost pressures.' The paper flags risk that 'demand levels, inflationary pressures or other forecast assumptions could deteriorate during Quarter two, resulting in additional financial pressure and a potential requirement for further reserve support.'
findings.matters: A 58% decline in reserves over one year significantly reduces financial flexibility and borrowing headroom. While £43m is a non-cash DSG accounting entry, the remaining £36m of real reserve use is substantial. The council's acknowledgement of deterioration risk indicates early forecasts may be optimistic.
findings.figures: Reserve decline from £137.5m to £58.4m (58% reduction); school reserves declining £43m; earmarked reserves declining £8m; grant reserves declining £28m
findings.quote: The total reserves balance on 31 March 2026 was £137.5m. During 2026/27, this is forecast to reduce to £58.4m.

findings.headline: Education, Health and Care Plans forecast to increase by 675 (17.8%), creating cascading pressures across children's placements, transport, and school funding
findings.detail: EHCPs are forecast to increase from 3,785 to 4,460, with the largest growth in profound needs category. This is creating a £8.617m pressure on mainstream top-up funding in schools, contributing to the £9m children's social care overspend, and driving a £3.7m home to school transport overspend. Government has not allocated funding through High Needs Stability Grant to support home to school transport costs, leaving the council bearing full exposure to the inflation and demand pressure.
findings.matters: This demonstrates a structural policy-driven shift in demand affecting multiple budget areas simultaneously. The council has limited control over EHCP issuance (a statutory entitlement) and must fund or manage service model changes across multiple directorate budgets in response to a single driver.
findings.figures: EHCP increase of 675 (+17.8%); £8.617m mainstream top-up pressure; £9m placements pressure; £3.7m transport pressure; transport inflation at 6.8% annual rate (ONS CPI June 2026)
findings.quote: Education, Health and Care Plans (EHCPs) are forecast to increase from 3,785 to 4,460, with the largest growth in the profound needs category, resulting in an additional £8.617m pressure on mainstream top-up funding.

findings.headline: Children's Services forecasting £9.4m overspend with £11.7m independent placement cost pressure despite £5m transformation programme savings
findings.detail: Independent placements have grown from 62 in November 2025 to 79 by June 2026. The service's transformation activities have delivered £5m of cost reductions and cost avoidance, but this has been overwhelmed by demand growth. The council notes placement forecasting is inherently volatile and that 'relatively small changes in the number of children requiring placements, the complexity of need, or the cost of individual placements can have a significant impact on the overall forecast.'
findings.matters: Demand-driven social care overspends are typically persistent and structural. The fact that a £5m transformation programme has been more than offset by continued demand growth indicates this will likely require sustained investment or service model change and signals a recurring budget issue.
findings.figures: £9.4m Children's Social Care overspend; £11.7m independent placement cost pressure; 79 active independent placements vs 62 in November 2025 (+27%); £5.0m transformation savings delivered
findings.quote: Detailed placement analysis indicates a total independent placement cost pressure of approximately £11.7m compared with the assumptions built into the 2026/27 budget.

findings.headline: High Needs Block forecasting £51.958m overspend with Dedicated Schools Grant deficit expected to grow from £25m to £54.3m
findings.detail: The schools budget is forecasting an overspend of £51.8m almost entirely within the High Needs Block. The DSG deficit is expected to increase from £25m (actual at March 2026) to £54.3m by March 2027, reflecting growth in Education, Health and Care Plans from 3,785 to 4,460. Government has indicated 90% of pre-March 2026 deficits will be supported through grant, conditional on councils submitting SEND Reform Plans.
findings.matters: DSG deficits are a balance-sheet liability that will persist across multiple years and affect financial sustainability. The scale and growth of Lincolnshire's deficit is consistent with national trends but represents a long-term pressure that cannot be resolved through in-year savings.
findings.figures: £51.958m High Needs Block overspend; DSG deficit forecast to grow from £25m to £54.3m; EHCPs increasing from 3,785 to 4,460
findings.quote: Most of the Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) pressure continues to fall within the High Needs Block, which is currently forecasting an overspend of £51.958m.

findings.headline: Council explicitly acknowledges 'underlying demand and cost pressures remain a key risk for 2026/27 and beyond'
findings.detail: Despite a £0.499m underspend in 2025/26, the council's own assessment is that underlying demand and cost pressures in social care services remain a key risk for future years. The council has built cost pressures into the 2026/27 budget but acknowledges 'risk from potentially higher demand increases than forecast'. This will be a key focus for Executive monitoring during 2026/27.
findings.matters: The council's risk assessment acknowledges it cannot reliably forecast demand-led cost growth in social care, suggesting future budget challenges are probable and may require difficult service decisions or reserve drawdown.
findings.figures: £0.499m underspend masks underlying structural pressures
findings.quote: While the outturn is positive, the underlying demand and cost pressures, remain a key risk for 2026/27 and beyond. These pressures were reflected in the 2026/27 budget; however, there remains risk from potentially higher demand increases than forecast.

findings.headline: Capital programme underspent by £50.201m (20%), primarily due to major project delays
findings.detail: The council invested £194.764m in capital during 2025/26, which was £50.201m lower than the planned £244.4m budget. The majority of underspend was due to timing of large-scale projects, particularly major infrastructure schemes such as Grantham Southern Relief Road and North Hykeham Relief Road. A full review of the capital programme is underway to reprofil timelines and costs.
findings.matters: Capital project delays can lead to construction cost inflation (typically 5-15% annually) and may signal delivery risks or resource constraints that could affect the council's ability to deliver planned infrastructure investment.
findings.figures: £50.201m underspend (20% of planned £244.4m); £194.764m actual capital investment
findings.quote: Overall, spending was £50.201 million lower than planned at year end, mainly due to changes in the timing of projects, with spend now expected to take place in future years.

findings.headline: Adult social care overspent by £5.450m despite achieving £4.7m planned savings due to demand growth
findings.detail: Adult social care experienced sustained demand growth that exceeded budget assumptions. During the year, 126 additional people entered direct payment arrangements and 7,158 additional hours of extra care were delivered. Community Supported Living client numbers doubled. Despite achieving approximately £4.7m planned savings plus an additional £1m through transformation, demand pressures overwhelmed these savings.
findings.matters: Demand growth outpacing savings delivery in a statutory service with ageing demographics signals structural affordability challenges that savings programmes cannot offset.
findings.figures: £5.450m overspend; 126 additional direct payment clients; 7,158 additional extra care hours; Community Supported Living numbers doubled
findings.quote: Services across adult social care reported an overspend of £5.450m, driven by several key pressures... During the year, 126 additional people entered direct payment arrangements and a further 7,158 hours of extra care were delivered.

findings.headline: Council used 100% of contingency budget to manage 2025/26 pressures, leaving no 2026/27 buffer
findings.detail: The council's £5.739m contingency funding was fully deployed to mitigate directorate overspends, with service-level cost pressures of £7.442m offset only by underspends in other budgets of £7.027m. Using all available contingency to balance the ordinary operating budget leaves no buffer for unexpected issues in 2026/27.
findings.matters: Zero contingency remaining signals underlying structural overspends that cannot be absorbed in future years and may require service reductions, reserve drawdown, or budget cuts.
findings.figures: £5.739m contingency used from £5.738m available; service overspends £7.442m offset by £7.027m underspends
findings.quote: Contingency funding played a key role in managing these pressures, with £5.739m of contingency mitigating directorate overspends.

findings.headline: Home to School Transport for SEND pupils surged 8.3%, driving £2.835m overspend
findings.detail: Transport Services overspent by £2.835m on Home to School Transport. SEND passenger numbers rose 8.3% in-year, far exceeding the MTFP assumption of 1.5% overall pupil growth. Actual pupil demand increased 3.9% (720 pupils), with SEND growth driven by increased complexity requiring specialist and single-occupancy journeys.
findings.matters: SEND transport costs are statutory and growing faster than expected due to increased complexity. This suggests ongoing structural pressure that will persist in future budgets.
findings.figures: £2.835m overspend; SEND passenger growth 8.3% vs 1.5% assumed overall; actual pupil growth 3.9% (720 pupils)
findings.quote: Transport Services reported a £2.835m overspend in 2025/26, driven predominantly by pressures within Home to School Transport where demand has grown significantly above assumptions, particularly for pupils with SEND. The MTFP assumed growth of 1.5% in pupil numbers (from 18,689 to 18,969); however, demand increased by 3.9% in-year (c. 720 pupils), with SEND passenger numbers rising by 8.3%

findings.headline: Adult social care equipment provider entered receivership mid-year, creating supply chain risk
findings.detail: Nottingham Rehab Limited (NRS Healthcare), the commissioned provider for the Lincolnshire Community Equipment Service, entered receivership during the year. The council implemented contingency arrangements and incurred £1.287m in additional mobilisation costs to maintain service delivery without interruption.
findings.matters: Provider insolvency in critical care services signals vulnerability in the care market and may indicate other commissioned services face similar pressures, creating unbudgeted costs and service continuity risks.
findings.figures: £1.287m additional mobilisation costs
findings.quote: Nottingham Rehab Limited (NRS Healthcare), the Council's commissioned provider for the Lincolnshire Community Equipment Service, entered receivership, creating a significant risk to the continuity of essential support for vulnerable residents. The Council acted swiftly, working with partners to implement contingency arrangements and maintain service delivery without interruption. These necessary actions resulted in additional mobilisation costs, contributing £1.287m to the overall overspend.

findings.headline: Children's residential placements 73% above budget (85 actual vs 49), driving £8.8m overspend
findings.detail: Children's Social Care had 799 children in care against a budget of 738. Specialist independent placements overspent by £8.824m (54.8% of budget), with residential care placements at 85 against a budget of 49. The overspend was driven by higher numbers and increasing complexity and cost of placements.
findings.matters: Persistent overspends in statutory services driven by 73% higher demand than budgeted indicates ongoing structural pressures unlikely to be resolved through service transformation.
findings.figures: 85 residential placements actual vs 49 budgeted; £8.824m overspend; 799 children in care vs 738 budgeted
findings.quote: The most significant pressure relates to specialist independent placements, overspending by £8.824m (54.8%), driven by: • Higher numbers in residential care with 85 placements compared to a budget of 49

findings.headline: High Needs Block has a structural deficit of £25.005m extending beyond 2025/26
findings.detail: The Dedicated Schools Grant overspent by £13.406m in 2025/26, driven by the High Needs block. Excluding school balances, this reflects a structural deficit of £25.005m carried forward. Government will support around 90% of deficits to 31 March 2026 through grant funding, but the council must manage the remaining residual risk through future financial planning.
findings.matters: A £25m structural deficit signals long-term unfunded liabilities that could affect creditworthiness and force difficult service or reserve decisions.
findings.figures: £13.406m overspend in 2025/26; £25.005m structural deficit; Government supporting ~90% of deficits
findings.quote: The Dedicated Schools Grant overspent by £13.406m, driven by continued pressure within the High Needs block. Excluding school balances, this reflects a structural deficit of £25.005m carried forward.

findings.headline: Finance function insourcing from 24-year Serco contract caused ERP processing delays and revealed unquestioned data quality issues.
findings.detail: The council insourced Finance and Payroll/HR from a 24-year Serco outsourcing arrangement, resulting in ERP processing delays. Post-integration analysis found Serco had met contractual KPIs through unsustainable overtime and temporary staffing. A lessons learned exercise identified that Serco had provided inaccurate data that the council did not challenge during transition. The council has proposed service reorganization and recommended data accuracy be incorporated into future contract management reviews.
findings.matters: Major service transitions expose gaps in supplier oversight and data validation controls; unchallenged data quality from external providers undermines financial reporting accuracy and operational decision-making.
findings.figures: 24-year outsourcing contract insourced; ERP processing delays documented upon integration
findings.quote: The lessons learned findings confirmed that inaccurate data had been shared with the Council prior to integration and that this data had not been challenged by the Council.

findings.headline: Council maintains £453.4m borrowings with negative cash position of £108.3m, indicating overdraft reliance that has worsened year-on-year.
findings.detail: Year-end borrowings of £453.4m (down from £462.1m prior year) are complemented by a negative cash position of (£108.3m), indicating overdraft use for daily cashflow. This overdraft has deteriorated from prior year's (£93.2m), showing increased reliance on short-term financing facilities.
findings.matters: High leverage combined with negative cash position and worsening overdraft dependency signals constrained liquidity and financial strain, critical factors in assessing lending risk and financial sustainability.
findings.figures: Year-end borrowings £453.4m (prior year £462.1m); cash position (£108.3m) negative (prior year (£93.2m))
findings.quote: Year-end borrowings £453.4m... Year-end cash position (£108.3m)

findings.headline: Council's usable reserves fell £43.5m to £274.7m, with earmarked reserves drawn down £37.1m and further planned use of £7.8m in 2025-26.
findings.detail: Usable reserves decreased £43.5m (13.7%) from £318.2m to £274.7m, primarily through £37.1m reduction in earmarked reserves to £159.3m. The general fund grew to £24.2m (up 47.6%), but overall reserves are declining despite planning. The council maintained its financial volatility reserve at £46.9m. The 2025-26 budget projects an additional £7.8m reserve use, indicating continued drawdown of financial buffers.
findings.matters: Planned but sustained reserve consumption indicates the council is using financial buffers to maintain service delivery, reducing medium-term financial resilience and strategic flexibility.
findings.figures: Usable reserves £274.7m (down from £318.2m); earmarked reserves £159.3m (down £37.1m); 2025-26 budgeted reserve use £7.8m
findings.quote: The Council's usable reserves have fallen by £43.5m (13.7%), this was largely driven by reduction of £37.1m in earmarked reserves.

findings.headline: Internal audit found 12 high-risk control deficiencies in procurement with inconsistent practices and incomplete documentation retention.
findings.detail: Internal audit's review of contracts and exceptions procedures identified 12 high-risk and 9 medium-risk recommendations. Investigation found varying procurement practices, inconsistent documentation retention, contracts not recorded in the central register, and interest declarations missing. External auditors tested five 2024-25 contracts and found no evidence of inappropriate assessment, but remediation is only 53% complete with 47% of actions still in progress.
findings.matters: Procurement control weaknesses risk inappropriate contracting decisions and inadequate governance oversight, affecting the council's ability to demonstrate value for money and proper stewardship of funds.
findings.figures: 12 high-risk recommendations, 9 medium-risk; 53% of remedial actions completed
findings.quote: Further investigation identified that varying practices were being followed within the procurement team and retention of documentation was inconsistent across contracts. This included numerous contracts not being recorded within the contract register and the documentation of interests not being retained.

findings.headline: Late government funding settlement created inherent risk of misinterpretation across the sector
findings.detail: The provisional settlement was published 17 December and final settlement 9 February, leaving a narrow window for councils to model impacts amid significant funding simplification. The document explicitly states: inherent general risk of misinterpretation or misunderstanding of some of the information. However, the council's position was ultimately found to be favourable.
findings.matters: A lender should understand that the council's budget was prepared under time pressure with novel funding structures. While the current position appears sound, the risk of misinterpretation was real. The council's approach appears to have been cautious.
findings.figures: Settlement published 17 December 2025 (provisional) and 9 February 2026 (final)
findings.quote: given the limited time and scale of information to fully work through including some information not yet published, there is an inherent general risk of misinterpretation or misunderstanding of some of the information across the sector

findings.headline: Pay award inflation estimated at £7.3m but actual amount to be determined later
findings.detail: The 2026/27 budget includes an estimate of £7.3m for pay award inflation, but the budget explicitly notes that the actual amount will depend on the 2026 pay award process outcome. This creates a risk of underprovision if the actual award exceeds the estimate.
findings.matters: A significant cost pressure (£7.3m represents material proportion of total pressures) is not yet fixed. Pay awards in recent years have tracked higher than historical norms, creating overspend risk.
findings.figures: £7.3m estimated; actual amount pending 2026 pay award process
findings.quote: This includes an estimate of pay award inflation in 2026/27 of £7.3m, noting that the actual amount will be determined by the 2026 pay award process.

findings.headline: Lincolnshire business rates pooling ends in 2026/27, eliminating source of growth income
findings.detail: The Lincolnshire business rates pool, which has allowed the council to benefit from growth in business rates across the pool, will not operate in 2026/27. This means no pooling gain this year. This is a direct loss of previously available income, though it is part of wider sector business rates reset.
